title: Pacific Western Airlines 501
summary: Pacific Western Airlines Flight 501 began takeoff from Calgary on runway 34 with 114 passengers and 5 crew. At 20 seconds into the takeoff, a loud popping sound occurred, the aircraft vibrated and veered left, and fire broke out in the rear. Pilot Stan Fleming successfully aborted the takeoff and emergency evacuation was ordered. The Canadian Aviation Safety Board determined that an uncontained failure of the left engine's 13th stage compressor disc caused debris to puncture a fuel cell, resulting in the fire. Five people were seriously injured and 22 others suffered minor injuries with no fatalities.

title: Vieques Air Link 901A
summary: Vieques Air Link Flight 901A, a Britten-Norman Islander, took off from Vieques Airport on August 2, 1984, with one pilot and eight passengers bound for Saint Croix. After takeoff, the aircraft lost altitude briefly before the pilot regained it momentarily; then the aircraft banked left and nosedived into the Atlantic Ocean. Investigation revealed the left fuel tank had been filled with water-contaminated fuel from an underground tank following days of heavy rain. The No. 1 engine failed after takeoff while the aircraft was over ocean. The pilot attempted to turn around but turned in the wrong direction, causing the aircraft to flip and crash into the water. The aircraft was also overloaded by 600 to 700 pounds over its maximum takeoff weight. All nine people on board were killed.
probable_cause: The accident resulted from fuel contamination in the left tank caused by water from recent heavy rains that reached an underground fuel storage tank, leading to No. 1 engine failure shortly after takeoff. The pilot's attempt to recover by turning around resulted in a turn in the wrong direction, causing loss of control. Contributing factors included the aircraft being overloaded by 600-700 pounds over maximum takeoff weight and the pilot being inadequately qualified for the position.

title: 1984 Biman Bangladesh Airlines Fokker F27 crash
summary: In poor weather with heavy rain and very low visibility, the crew attempted a VOR approach to runway 32 but missed the runway and executed a missed approach. A second missed approach was executed on an ILS approach to runway 14 as both pilots failed to spot the runway. On the third approach, the aircraft descended too low while still several hundred meters from the runway, but neither crew member realized this due to poor visibility, and the aircraft crashed into a swamp about 550 meters short of the runway.

title: Aeroservicios Ecuatorianos 767-103
summary: Aeroservicios Ecuatorianos Flight 767-103, a Douglas DC-8-55F cargo jet, failed to become airborne during takeoff from Quito and struck an ILS antenna at the runway end before hitting several houses. The investigation found the horizontal stabilizer was set incorrectly at 0.5 degrees nose up instead of 8 degrees, requiring excessive distance to rotate. Crew labor disputes and incorrect departure clearance procedures also contributed.

title: PBA 1039
summary: PBA Flight 1039 received takeoff clearance and began the takeoff roll from Runway 31. Thirty seconds after takeoff, witnesses saw the aircraft in a steep descent. title: Aeroflot 3519
summary: Two minutes after takeoff at 2,040 meters, the No. 3 engine failed due to a metallurgical defect in the compressor disk and caught fire. The flight engineer mistakenly shut down the No. 2 engine instead of the failed No. 3 engine. The fire spread to the pylon and auxiliary power unit, destroying the electrical and hydraulic systems. The aircraft crashed into the runway at a 50-degree angle. One passenger survived with severe injuries.
probable_cause: Engine failure due to metallurgical defect in first stage low pressure compressor disk, compounded by the flight engineer shutting down the wrong engine, and subsequent fire spread through the aircraft.

factors.evidence: Two minutes and one second into the flight, at a speed of 480 km/h and an altitude of 2040 m, the No. 3 (starboard) engine failed and caught fire. This was due to a metallurgical and manufacturing defect in the first stage low pressure compressor disk.
The flight engineer mistakenly shut down the No. 2 (center) engine; ten seconds later, he realized his error and attempted to restart it.
By that time, the fire from the No. 3 engine had spread to the pylon and the auxiliary power unit in the rear compartment and continued to spread to the No. 2 engine.
The fire damaged the aircraft's electrical system, causing the voltage to drop and the hydraulics to fail.
Due to the extensive fire damage that left the aircraft with only one functional engine, the crew was unable to control the plane.
the fire from the No. 3 engine had spread to the pylon and the auxiliary power unit
